<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Alma S. Adams, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: INTRODUCTION
The Charter School Program (CSP) is authorized by the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965 (ESEA)\1\ for the purpose of ``supporting innovation; providing financial assistance for the planning, design, and initial implementation of charter schools; increasing the number of high-quality charter schools; encouraging states to provide charter schools facilities financing; and strengthening the charter school authorizing process.''\2\ H.R. 7086, the Equitable Access to School Facilities Act, introduced by Rep. Juan Ciscomani (R- AZ),\3\ would expand the role of state entities by requiring them to establish revolving loans for school facilities. It would also replace an existing program that supports charter school facilities by providing grants to states on a per-pupil basis with a new program. Unfortunately, H.R. 7086 would make these changes at the expense of transparency, accountability, and oversight, as well as by taking funding away from charter school classrooms and students.
\1\20 U.S.C. Sec. Sec. 7221-7221j.
\2\Rebecca R. Skinner & Isobel Sorenson, Cong. Rsch. Serv., IF12601, ESEA: Charter Schools Program, (2024), https://www.crs.gov/ Reports/IF12601; see 20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221(1)-(8).
\3\Equitable Access to School Facilities Act, H.R. 7086, 119th Cong. (2026).
BACKGROUND
Pursuant to current law, CSP supports charter schools in three ways, and each of these ways has its own specific funding set-aside/reservation.\4\ The first is supporting high-quality charter schools (with a set-aside of 65% of CSP funds), which provides grants to state entities that in turn provide subgrants to charter school developers to start new charter schools and replicate and expand high-quality charter schools.\5\ The second is providing facilities financing assistance (with a set-aside of 12.5% of CSP funds) in the form of either Credit Enhancement Grants ``to public or private entities (or a combination of the two) for the development of credit enhancement initiatives to assist charter schools in acquiring, constructing, or renovating facilities''\6\ or in the form of Facilities Incentives Grants that provide eligible state entities with ``per-pupil facilities allowances to help charter schools obtain facilities.''\7\ The third is national activities (with a set-aside of 22.5% of CSP funds), which are grants used to support replication and expansion of high-quality charter schools by charter management organizations,\8\ developer grants,\9\ and grants for evaluations and dissemination of best practices.\10\ All of these different funding tranches support charter schools, which are public, independently run schools that operate with public funds.\11\
\4\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221a(b); Skinner, supra note 2.
\5\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221b.
\6\Skinner, supra note 2; 20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221c(a).
\7\Skinner, supra note 2; 20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221c(k).
\8\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221d(a)(1); Skinner, supra note 2.
\9\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221d(a)(2); Skinner, supra note 2.
\10\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221d(a)(3); Skinner, supra note 2.
\11\Skinner, supra note 2.
SUMMARY OF CONCERNS
H.R. 7086 Would Snatch Funding from Students and Classrooms and Instead
Use that Funding for Facilities
The Bill Would Expand the Role of State Entities Without
Additional Support
Under the supporting high-quality charter schools section of CSP, state entities must use not less than 90 percent of grant funds for subgrants to charter school developers to open new charter schools or replicate or expand high-quality charter schools.\12\ The remaining grant funds must be used by the state to provide technical assistance and improve authorizing quality (not less than seven percent) and for administrative costs (not less than three percent).\13\ Thus, the overwhelming bulk of the funding is currently used to open schools, create classrooms, and serve students. H.R. 7086 would reduce the amount of funding available for opening, replication, or expanding charter schools from at least 90 percent to at least 80 percent. It would require that the ten percent reduction be used by state entities to instead establish a revolving loan fund to provide loans to eligible applicants to (1) assist them in their operations, or (2) help them obtain, renovate, or rehabilitate facilities for new or existing charter schools within the state. H.R. 7086 would further expand the role of state entities by authorizing them to assist in locating and accessing facilities for charter schools as well as provide one-time assistance to a future or current charter school to bring its facility into compliance with state and local building codes and regulations. These changes would expand the role of state entities into entirely new areas, without providing additional funding, guidance, or expertise. Moreover, the reduction in funding would directly reduce the amount of funding available for schools, classrooms, and students.
\12\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221b(c)(1)(A).
\13\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221b(c)(1).
The Bill Would Enable Facilities Costs to Consume Subgrants
Current law permits eligible applicants that receive a subgrant for supporting high-quality charter schools to use funding for ``necessary renovations'' of a ``new school building'' to ensure it complies ``with applicable statutes and regulations'' as well as ``minor facilities repairs (excluding construction).''\14\ H.R. 7086 would substantially expand this to include ``repairs, renovations, and building out of charter school facilities'' to ensure compliance; however, the term ``building out'' is not defined and its meaning is unclear, thereby lacking any guardrails or parameters. Moreover, the bill would strike language in current law limiting use of this funding to new buildings and minor facilities repairs as well as the prohibition against construction. With these changes, the bill would dramatically expand the allowable use of funds to support major facilities changes and brick and mortar construction, the costs of which could quickly consume all available funding that would otherwise be used to support high-quality charter schools.
\14\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221b(h)(3).
H.R. 7086 Would Cap Reporting Requirements Under Credit Enhancement
Grants
Credit Enhancement Grants help charter schools acquire, construct, and renovate facilities by assisting them in acquiring financing instruments such as loans and bonds. In essence, grants are made to eligible entities that then establish reserve accounts that are used to leverage private financing. The term of the grant is usually ``until the Federal funds and earnings on those funds have been expended for the grant purposes or until financing facilitated by the grant has been retired, whichever is later.''\15\ Current law requires that the eligible entity submit an annual report to the Secretary for the duration of the grant, specifies what must be included in the report, and requires the Secretary to submit to Congress an annual comprehensive report of all such reports.\16\ H.R. 7086 would narrow reporting requirements under the Credit Enhancement Grants Program by capping the number of years that grantees must submit annual reports. Doing so would reduce transparency and oversight and permit unchecked spending of taxpayer dollars.
\15\See, e.g., 90 Fed. Reg. 21017 (May 16, 2025).
\16\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221c(h)(2).
H.R. 7086 Would Waive Federal Requirements Applicable to the Federal
Interest in Charter School Facilities Funded with Taxpayer
Dollars
The federal government has an interest in ensuring that federal funds, including awards and grants, are used pursuant to federal law for their intended purpose; as a result, an agency providing grants carries with it a responsibility for continued supervision over that funding. Thus, the federal government has a continued interest in the funding in the form of an equitable lien due to the continued supervision of those funds by the agency that provided them. This includes an interest in ``[r]eal property, equipment, and intangible property acquired or improved'' using federal awards or grants,\17\ and a requirement exists ``to submit reports on the status of real property in which the Federal Government retains an interest.''\18\ The Code of Federal Regulations includes requirements that relate to this federal interest.\19\ As a result, school facilities acquired or improved using a federal grant are subject to a federal interest/equitable lien and to the reporting requirement.
\17\2 C.F.R. Sec. 200.316 (2026).
\18\2 C.F.R. Sec. 200.330 (2026).
\19\2 C.F.R. Sec. 200.1 (2026).
H.R. 7086 would exempt any property relating to charter school facilities from being subject to the recording and reporting requirements of this federal interest. This would unfairly elevate charter schools above all other types of grantees that use federal funding to acquire property; charter schools would not be subject to the same requirements as all other grantees who use federal funding to acquire property. This also would effectively waive accountability for taxpayer dollars used in the acquisition and improvement of charter schools. While federal regulations do provide discretion on whether the interest must be recorded,\20\ no such discretion is provided with regard to the reporting requirement. Thus, H.R. 7086 would unfairly exempt charter schools from federal regulations and elevate them above all other taxpayer interests in real property. Instead, current law should be maintained; the interest in charter schools should not be waived and should be reported as required under federal regulations.
\20\2 C.F.R. Sec. 200.316 (2026).
H.R. 7086 Would Replace Per-Pupil Facilities Grants with a New Program
with No Evaluation or Oversight
H.R. 7086 would eliminate the Per-Pupil Facilities Aid Program in current law and replace it with a new State Facilities Aid Program. The new grant program would provide funding to state entities, on a competitive basis, to aid in the need for charter school facilities. However, the allowable uses of funds would be much broader than under current law.
In this new grant program, grants could be used to fund or create financing for acquiring, leasing, or renovating facilities, as well as ongoing facilities costs. This would create no incentive to plan for or provide for future facilities costs. Grants could also be used for ``the creation of alternative ownership models, to plan, develop, and manage facilities for charter school.''\21\ No explanation or parameters are provided for what these alternative ownership models would look like. Furthermore, funds under the new grant program could be shifted and used to establish, maintain, or supplement a reserve account under the Credit Enhancement program. This may be done either by establishing and maintaining a reserve account in states that did not receive a Credit Enhancement Grant or by further funding a reserve account in states that did receive a Credit Enhancement Grant.
\21\H.R. 7086 Sec. 2, 119th Cong. (2026).
Under the new program, the federal share of the State Facilities Aid Program would remain constant at 60 percent each year of the grant. This would constitute a significant change from current law, which requires the federal share to be reduced each year over five years, such that by the fifth year the federal share is only 20 percent. H.R. 7086 would eliminate the incentive to increase the non-federal share of the grant and would instead place a permanent financial burden on the federal government. In addition, the new program would permit the non-federal share of the grant to be funded in whole or in part by one or more other organizations, with no specifications on the types of organizations.
